[[File:Tétragone cornue3.jpg|thumb|Tétragone cornue in "Les plantes potagères" Vilmorin 1925]]
'''''Tetragonia tetragonioides''''', commonly called '''New Zealand spinach''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref><ref>{{PLANTS|id=Tete3|taxon=Tetragonia tetragonioides|accessdate=19 January 2018}}</ref> '''warrigal greens''' or by its [[Māori language|Māori]] name of '''Kōkihi''', is a flowering plant in the fig-marigold family ([[Aizoaceae]]). It is often cultivated as a leafy vegetable.

It is a widespread species, native to eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. It has been introduced and is an [[invasive species]] in many parts of Africa, Europe, North America, and South America.<ref name="cabi">{{cite web | url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/52942 | title=Tetragonia tetragonioides | publisher=Invasive Species Compendium}}</ref> Its natural habitat is sandy shorelines and bluffs, often in disturbed areas.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200007018 ''Tetragonia tetragonioides''] Flora of North America</ref> It is a [[halophyte]] and grows well in [[soil salinity|saline ground]].

==Description==
The plant has a trailing habit, and will form a thick carpet on the ground or climb through other vegetation and hang downwards. It can have erect growth when young.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200007018 ''Tetragonia tetragonioides''] Flora of China</ref> The leaves of the plant are {{Convert|3-15|cm|abbr=on}} long, triangular in shape, and bright green. The leaves are thick, and covered with tiny [[wikt:Papillae|papillae]] that look like waterdrops on the top and bottom of the leaves. The [[flower]]s of the plant are yellow,<ref name=RBGDT/> and the [[fruit]] are small, hard capsules each with 4–10 horned seeds.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lehnebach |first=Carlos A. |url=https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q115065494 |title=Native Plants of Aotearoa |last2=Meudt |first2=Heidi |date=2022-10-01 |publisher=Te Papa Press |isbn=978-1-9911509-3-6 |series=Te Papa Te Taiao Nature Series |pages=45 |language=English}}</ref>

[[Raphides|Sphaeraphides]] are found in at least the leaves, [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] and ovary.{{sfn|Gulliver|1864|p=251}}

==Taxonomy==
Prussian naturalist [[Peter Simon Pallas|Peter Pallas]] described the species as ''Demidovia tetragonoides'' in 1781.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pallas |first1=Peter Simon |title=Enumeratio plantarum quae in hortoi viri illustris atque escell. Dni. Procopi a Demidof. |date=1781 |publisher=Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences | language=Russian |location=Saint Petersburg |pages=151–157 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k96903s/f184.image}}</ref> German botanist [[Otto Kuntze]] placed the species in the genus ''Tetragonia'' in his 1891 work ''[[Revisio Generum Plantarum]]'', resulting in its current binomial name.<ref name="Kuntz1891">{{cite book|last=Kuntze|first=Otto|authorlink=Otto Kuntze|title=Revisio Generum Plantarum |volume=v.2|publisher=A. Felix|location=Leipzig, Germany|year=1891|page=264|url=https://biodiversitylibrary.org/page/127724}}</ref>

This widely distributed plant has many common names, depending on its location. In addition to the name New Zealand spinach, it is also known as [[Botany Bay]] spinach, Cook's cabbage, {{Lang|mi|kōkihi}} (in [[Māori language|Māori]]), sea spinach, and tetragon. Its Australian names of Warrigal Greens and Warrigal Cabbage<ref name=RBGDT/> come from the local use of ''[[wikt:warrigal|warrigal]]'' to describe plants that are wild (not farmed originally).<ref>{{cite book |title=The New Oxford American Dictionary |edition=3rd |date=2012 | quote =adjective (of a plant) not cultivated: ''warrigal melons''.}}</ref>

==Cultivation==

It is grown for the [[List of plants with edible leaves|edible leaves]], and can be used as food or an [[ornamental plant]] for ground cover. It can be an annual or perennial.<ref name="cabi" /> As some of its names signify, it has similar flavour and texture properties to [[spinach]], and is cooked like spinach. Like spinach, it contains [[oxalate]]s; its medium to low levels of oxalates need to be removed by [[blanching (cooking)|blanching]] the leaves in hot water<ref name="bushtucker">{{cite web| url=http://media.smh.com.au/life-and-style/essentials/hungry-try-some-bush-tucker-2457561.html| type=movie| title=Hungry? Try some bush tucker| date=2011-06-28| publisher=The Sydney Morning Herald| accessdate=2011-06-28| archive-date=2011-06-29| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629221549/http://media.smh.com.au/life-and-style/essentials/hungry-try-some-bush-tucker-2457561.html| url-status=dead}}</ref> for one minute, then rinsing in cold water before cooking. It thrives in hot weather, and is considered an [[heirloom vegetable]]. Few insects consume it, and even [[slug]]s and [[snail]]s do not seem to feed on it.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Barkla |first=Bronwyn |date=2019-02-23 |title=Warrigal greens are tasty, salty, and covered in tiny balloon-like hairs |url=http://theconversation.com/warrigal-greens-are-tasty-salty-and-covered-in-tiny-balloon-like-hairs-112307 |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref>

The thick, irregularly-shaped [[seed]]s should be planted just after the last spring [[frost]]. Before planting, the seeds should be soaked for 12 hours in cold water, or 3 hours in warm water. Seeds should be planted {{convert|5|-|10|mm|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} deep, and spaced {{convert|15|-|30|cm|abbr=on}} apart. The seedlings will emerge in 10–20 days, and it will continue to produce greens through the summer. Mature plant will self-seed. Seeds will overwinter up to USDA zone 5.{{Citation needed|date=February 2020}}

==As food==
The species, rarely used by indigenous people as a [[leaf vegetable]], was first documented by [[James Cook|Captain Cook]]. It was immediately picked, cooked, and [[pickling|pickled]] to help fight [[scurvy]], and taken with the crew of the [[HM Bark Endeavour|''Endeavour'']].<ref name=RBGDT>{{cite web |title=Tetragonia tetragonioides |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/education/Resources/bush_foods/Tetragonia_tetragonioides |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust |accessdate=10 February 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140209094629/http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/education/Resources/bush_foods/Tetragonia_tetragonioides |archivedate=9 February 2014 }}</ref> It spread when the explorer and botanist [[Joseph Banks]] took seeds back to [[Kew Gardens]] during the latter half of the 18th century.<ref>Low, T., ''Wild Food Plants of Australia'', Angus & Robertson, 1991, {{ISBN|0-207-16930-6}}</ref> For two centuries, ''T. tetragonioides'' was the only cultivated vegetable to have originated from Australia and New Zealand.{{Citation needed|date=November 2019}}

There are some indications that Māori did eat {{Lang|mi|kōkihi}} perhaps more regularly. According to Murdoch Riley, "to counteract the bitterness of the older leaves of this herb, the Māori boiled it with the roots of the convolvulus (''pōhue'')", in reference to species of [[Convolvulaceae]] now classified as ''[[Calystegia]]''.<ref>{{cite book|url=http://maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/PeoplePlantsDetails.aspx?PKey=1e64103c-55a7-45a1-bd2c-8603f012fa17|last=Riley|first=Murdoch|year=1994|title=Maori Healing and Herbal|location=Paraparaumu, New Zealand|publisher=Viking Sevenseas N.Z. Ltd.|pages=7–10|isbn=0854670955}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://christchurchcitylibraries.com/Maori/Rongoa/|title=Māori Healing and Herbal - New Zealand Ethnobotanical Sourcebook|publisher=Viking Sevenseas NZ Ltd|year=1994|page=221}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=pōhue - Māori Dictionary|url=https://maoridictionary.co.nz/word/5723|access-date=2021-05-09|website=maoridictionary.co.nz}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Māori Plant Use Database Plant Use Details of Calystegia sepium|url=https://maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/PeoplePlantsDetails.aspx?PKey=95a32b43-03fd-4429-a1b1-98c33c6a30a7|access-date=2021-05-09|website=maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz}}</ref> The tips of the spinach can be pinched off and eaten raw or cooked.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=135 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA135}}</ref>

==Nutrition==
When consumed after [[boiling]], New Zealand spinach is 95% water, 2% [[carbohydrate]]s, 1% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and contains negligible [[fat]], while supplying only 12 [[calorie]]s (table). In a reference amount of {{cvt|100|g}}, the spinach is particularly rich in [[vitamin K]], providing 243% of the [[Daily Value]] (DV). It also contains appreciable amounts of [[vitamin B6|vitamin B<sub>6</sub>]], [[vitamin C]], and [[manganese in biology|manganese]] (14–23% DV) (table).
